intro: Dutch elm disease never reached Australia, so Melbourne still has elms of a size and age Europe lost, and one of them anchors this page. Sixteen trees here, two separate afternoons. Seven stand within about 1.7 kilometres of each other in the small parks of Carlton North, Fitzroy North and Clifton Hill, three kilometres north of the CBD. The other nine run from Burnley Gardens, a free university botanic garden on the Yarra, out along Yarra Boulevard and on to Madden Grove: eucalypts, a hoop pine, a peppercorn tree and the oldest dated tree in the city.
meta_description: Melbourne's old trees stand in the parks north of the CBD and in Burnley Gardens: a 135-year-old English elm, a fig on a filled quarry, three red gums.
question_meta: Melbourne's oldest dated tree is an Osage orange on Yarra Boulevard, dated to the 1860s. Where it stands, and fifteen more of the city's registered trees.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Melbourne that anyone has put a date on is the Osage Orange of Yarra Boulevard, in Yarra Bend Park at Burnley, dated to the 1860s and so around 160 years old. The Victorian Heritage Database's citation for the Boulevard Parklands records an Osage orange north-east of the point where Yarra Boulevard meets Swan Street and puts it in that decade; the City of Yarra's significant tree register lists one at the same spot, 27 metres tall and 169 centimetres of diameter at breast height, roughly 5.31 metres round. That is a claim about the best-dated tree rather than the oldest thing growing in the city: eleven of the sixteen trees on this page carry only the register's band of over a hundred years, with no year attached at all, and a 2015 account of Burnley Gardens describes a river red gum there believed to exceed 400 years without tying the claim to a particular trunk.
question_context: This page is built on the City of Yarra's significant tree register, walked in 2012, and two things about that source shape everything here. It publishes the diameter of a trunk at breast height rather than the circumference, so every girth quoted on this page is a conversion. And its age field is a set of bands rather than years: eleven of these sixteen trees carry nothing more precise than over a hundred years. The dates that do exist come from elsewhere. The National Trust of Australia dated the English elm in Darling Gardens at about 120 years in February 2011, making it roughly 135 now, and the Victorian Heritage Database puts the Osage orange on Yarra Boulevard in the 1860s, which is why that tree carries the answer. One rival claim cannot be checked: a 2015 account of Burnley Gardens describes a river red gum believed to exceed 400 years, but nobody has matched it to a trunk. The Osage orange sits on the second of two walks here, nine trees from Burnley Gardens to Madden Grove; the other seven are three kilometres north of the CBD. See the full list on the Melbourne page.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Melbourne?
faq.a: The Osage Orange of Yarra Boulevard, in Yarra Bend Park at Burnley. The Victorian Heritage Database dates it to the 1860s, which makes it around 160 years old. Eleven of the sixteen trees on this page carry no year at all, only the city register's band of over a hundred years. A 2015 account of Burnley Gardens describes a river red gum believed to be over 400 years old, but nobody has tied that to a particular trunk, so it is not the answer here.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, every one of them. They stand in public parks and public parkland with no gate and no ticket: Curtain Square, Edinburgh Gardens, Darling Gardens, the Boulevard Parklands along the Yarra, Madden Grove in Richmond Park, and Burnley Gardens, a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus that anyone can walk into.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Not all sixteen, but the page splits into two walks, seven trees and nine. Curtain Square, Edinburgh Gardens and Darling Gardens run in a line through Carlton North, Fitzroy North and Clifton Hill, about 1.7 kilometres end to end and roughly three kilometres from the CBD. The second walk starts in Burnley Gardens, where four of the trees stand within a few hundred metres of each other, follows Yarra Boulevard out to the Osage orange and the river red gum in Yarra Bend Park, and continues on to the peppercorn and the lemon-scented gum in Madden Grove, Richmond, about 1.5 kilometres further.

The holm oak in Edinburgh Gardens, at 177 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which is about 5.56 metres around. The City of Yarra measures across the trunk rather than around it, so every girth on this page is a conversion.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Curtain Square

location.address: Curtain Square, Canning Street entrance, Carlton North VIC 3054

trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park (also used as an off-leash dog area).
trees.transport: Curtain Square/Rathdowne St bus stop is directly outside; tram route 96 on Nicholson Street is roughly a 5-10 minute walk.
trees.story: This park was a hole in the ground, and prisoners dug it. Between 1853 and 1866 the block was a bluestone quarry worked by men from the Collingwood Stockade, and bluestone is the rock Melbourne's kerbs and laneways are still made of. The pit was filled, levelled and planted, and Curtain Square became a square. This fig went in somewhere after that. It is a Moreton Bay fig, Ficus macrophylla, an Australian tree but not a Melbourne one: its home range runs up the east coast around Moreton Bay in Queensland, roughly 1,400 kilometres north, and Victorian gardeners planted it down here anyway for the shade and the ropey buttress roots. It stands 25 metres tall with a trunk of about 4.77 metres round, converted from the 152 centimetres of diameter at breast height the City of Yarra's register publishes, because the register measures across the trunk rather than around it. Local accounts describe a surviving avenue of Moreton Bay figs at the Canning Street entrance, which is where this tree stands. Whether this particular trunk belongs to that avenue is not something anyone has written down. Its age is the register's own band, over a hundred years at the survey in August 2012, and there is no planting date on record. If you know one, tell us.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 180)
City of Yarra Heritage Review, Landscape Citations (local significance listing for Curtain Square, referenced via search; full citation PDF not fetched this pass)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its ropey, buttressed roots spreading from a trunk about 4.77 metres round. It stands near the Canning Street entrance of Curtain Square, Carlton North.

trees.name: The London Plane of Curtain Square
trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park.
trees.transport: Curtain Square/Rathdowne St bus stop is directly outside; tram route 96 on Nicholson Street is roughly a 5-10 minute walk.
trees.story: The most recent evidence that this tree is standing is from 2012. The City of Yarra's arborists surveyed Curtain Square in August of that year and recorded a London plane on the Rathdowne Street side of the park: 24 metres tall, 170 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to roughly 5.34 metres of girth, since the register publishes the width across a trunk rather than the measure around it. Only one trunk on this page is heavier, the holm oak in Edinburgh Gardens. The age band on the record is 81 to 100 years, putting the planting somewhere in the decade after the First World War and the tree at roughly a century now. Nothing newer than that survey turned up. Squares here do lose trees: in 2017 Curtain Square's avenue of elms, some of them about a hundred years old, was cut down on safety grounds and replaced with scarlet oaks. That was a different avenue and a different species, and nothing suggests this plane was touched. Still, if you walk through, look and tell us what is there. London plane is a hybrid of an American and an oriental parent, crossed in the seventeenth century, and it turned out to shrug off soot, drought and butchered roots better than anything else, which is why it lines streets on five continents including this one.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 190)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its thick trunk, about 5.34 metres round, one of the heaviest on this page. It stands on the Rathdowne Street side of Curtain Square, Carlton North.

trees.name: The Finer Holm Oak of Edinburgh Gardens

location.address: Edinburgh Gardens, near the bowling club, off Brunswick Street, Fitzroy North VIC 3068

trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park, 24 hectares, unrestricted access per the National Trust record.
trees.transport: Rushall railway station (Mernda line) is about a 3 minute walk from the gardens; tram route 11/112 runs along nearby St Georges Road.
trees.story: Edinburgh Gardens has two holm oaks, and the National Trust of Australia has a view about which one to look at. Its Significant Tree Register calls this the finer of the two examples of the species in the gardens, and it is certainly the heavier: the City of Yarra records 177 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which is about 5.56 metres of girth, since that 177 is a width across the trunk and not a measurement around it. That is the thickest trunk here and a record nowhere else: the Trust's own significance statement points to a tree at Talindert, near Camperdown in western Victoria, as the biggest of its kind in Victoria. This one is about 20 metres tall and stands near the bowling club. The same Trust survey, in 2011, recorded its condition as poor and noted that it is overcrowded by nearby elms. Those elms are worth knowing about. Dutch elm disease never reached Australia, and Edinburgh Gardens holds one of the most significant stands of mature elms left in the world, trees of a size Britain and Europe stopped having half a century ago. The oak has been growing up inside all of that. Its age is the register's band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey, with no planting year on record.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 120)
https://trusttrees.org.au/tree/VIC/Fitzroy_North/Edinburgh_Gardens_Brunswick_Street (National Trust of Australia Vic, Significant Tree Register)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, about 5.56 metres round, the thickest on this page, crowded close by nearby elms. It stands near the bowling club in Edinburgh Gardens, Fitzroy North.

trees.name: The Remnant River Red Gum of Edinburgh Gardens
trees.age_estimate: over 100 years, possibly a remnant predating the park

location.address: Edinburgh Gardens, off Brunswick Street/Alfred Crescent, Fitzroy North VIC 3068

trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park.
trees.transport: Rushall railway station (Mernda line) is about a 3 minute walk from the gardens; tram route 11/112 runs along nearby St Georges Road.
trees.story: Queen Victoria granted this ground to the people of Fitzroy in 1862. The river red gum may have been standing here already. The City of Yarra's register classes it as remnant, the category it uses for indigenous vegetation that was left rather than planted, and tags the same entry outstanding size, particularly old and significant habitat value. What the register does not give is a year. Its age band is the coarse one, over a hundred years at the survey in August 2012, and no independent source names this individual tree, so how much of this site's history it actually saw is an open question. If you know of a heritage citation or an old photograph that dates it, we would like to see it. The measurements are firmer: 28 metres tall, and 138 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which works out at roughly 4.33 metres of girth, since Yarra publishes the width across a trunk rather than the way round it. Eucalyptus camaldulensis is the most widely spread eucalypt in Australia, the tree of inland rivers and creek beds, and it has a habit of shedding heavy limbs in still weather, which is part of what makes an old one in a public park unusual. Most of what grows in these 24 hectares was brought in and planted. This one may not have been.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 104)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the park's remnant native tree, left standing rather than planted when this ground was granted to Fitzroy in 1862. It stands off Brunswick Street, Edinburgh Gardens.

trees.name: The English Elm of Darling Gardens

location.address: Darling Gardens, off Gold Street, Clifton Hill VIC 3068

trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park (also used as an off-leash dog area, does not restrict general access).
trees.transport: Clifton Hill railway station (Hurstbridge/Mernda lines) is about a 6 minute walk; tram route 86 on Queens Parade is about a 6 minute walk (24-Gold St/Queens Pde stop).
trees.story: The English elm barely exists as a mature tree in England any more. Melbourne kept its. Dutch elm disease killed elms across Britain and Europe by the tens of millions from the 1960s on and never reached Australia, which left this city holding elm plantings of an age and size Europe lost. The National Trust of Australia dated this one at about 120 years in February 2011, so roughly 135 now, and calls it an outstanding example of the species. It stands 28 metres tall at the Gold Street end of Darling Gardens, and the City of Yarra's register gives it 154 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which is 4.84 metres of girth: the register's figure is a diameter, so every girth on this page is a conversion from one. The two registers disagree about the name. Yarra records it as Ulmus minor 'Atinia'; the Trust's entry says Ulmus procera. Both mean English elm, and botanists have spent decades arguing over whether they are one tree or two. Darling Gardens was permanently reserved in 1866 and laid out with elms and oaks in the 1890s. The Trust's dating puts this tree's planting in that same decade, which is arithmetic rather than a record: nothing ties this trunk to that scheme by name.

best_time.label: April and May, when the elm turns yellow

verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 1)

National Trust of Australia (Vic) Significant Tree Register, cited via search snippet (trusttrees.org.au covers Darling Gardens; direct fetch not completed this pass) and corroborated by Collingwood Historical Society, https://collingwoodhs.org.au/darling-gardens-clifton-hill-52103/
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 28 metres tall with a trunk over 150 centimetres across, rare now that Dutch elm disease has taken most of Europe's old elms. It stands at the Gold Street end of Darling Gardens.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Darling Gardens

location.address: Darling Gardens, off Gold Street, Clifton Hill VIC 3068

trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park.
trees.transport: Clifton Hill railway station (Hurstbridge/Mernda lines) is about a 6 minute walk; tram route 86 on Queens Parade is about a 6 minute walk (24-Gold St/Queens Pde stop).
trees.story: Darling Gardens has two trees on the National Trust's register. This is the other one. The Trust names a holm oak of regional significance alongside the elm, and it is much the smaller of the pair: 84 centimetres of diameter at breast height in the City of Yarra's survey, roughly 2.64 metres of girth once converted from the width across the trunk that the register publishes, against the elm's 4.84. It stands 16 metres tall about ninety metres from the elm, nearer the middle of the park than the Gold Street corner. Size is plainly not why it is listed. Quercus ilex is the evergreen oak of the Mediterranean, dark, leathery and dense enough that little grows under it, and it holds its canopy through the entire year. In a Melbourne February that is the difference between shade and no shade, and in July, when the elms around it are bare, it is still in full leaf. Spain and Portugal have grazed pigs on the acorns of this species for centuries, which is the other reason it travelled as far as it did. The age on file is the register's blunt band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey, with no year and no independent date behind it. If you know when Darling Gardens' oak went in, tell us.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 2)

National Trust of Australia (Vic) Significant Tree Register, cited via search snippet: 'Darling Gardens has two trees on the register: a holm oak (Quercus ilex) of regional significance ... and an English elm'
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its dark, dense, evergreen canopy, still in full leaf when the nearby elms are bare. It stands about ninety metres from Darling Gardens' registered elm, off Gold Street.

trees.name: The River Red Gum of Burnley Gardens

location.address: Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne Burnley campus, 500 Yarra Boulevard, Burnley VIC 3121

trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
The city register gives this tree a hundred years. A local account of the same garden gives one of its red gums four hundred.

The register is the firmer of the two. The City of Yarra surveyed Burnley Gardens on 4 October 2012 and recorded a river red gum of 17 metres and 92 centimetres of diameter at breast height, about 2.89 metres of girth once converted, since the register measures across a trunk rather than around it. It tagged the entry remnant, which is its word for indigenous vegetation left standing rather than planted, alongside outstanding size, particularly old and significant habitat value. The age field is the coarse one: over a hundred years, no year attached.

The other figure comes from a 2015 account of Burnley's Native Garden, which describes a river red gum in the south-west corner believed to exceed 400 years and to predate the European settlement of this ground. Nobody has tied that description to a particular trunk, and the Native Garden may hold more than one old red gum, so both numbers stand here and we pick neither. If you know which tree that account means, we would like to hear it.

What is not in doubt is the setting. The tree stands on a bend of the Yarra, on the sort of ground where Eucalyptus camaldulensis was growing long before anyone laid a garden over it.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 228): dbh 92cm, height 17m, significance 'Significant Habitat Value, Outstanding Size, Remnant, Particularly Old', surveyed 2012-10-04

Gardendrum, 'Burnley's Secret Botanic Garden Part 3' (gardendrum.com/2015/07/11): describes a River Red Gum in the southwest corner of Burnley Gardens' Native Garden believed to exceed 400 years old and to pre-date European colonisation of the site. Corroborates species, remnant status and general location (Native Garden, Burnley Gardens) but does NOT confirm this is the same individual tree as register ref 228; treat as a plausible but unconfirmed match, not proof.

iNaturalist: Eucalyptus camaldulensis observations within the Burnley campus grounds as recently as 2025-05-20 (obs 282527453, ~380m away, needs_id) confirm the species is present and alive in the immediate area, though not pinned to this exact tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing as remnant, pre-garden vegetation rather than a planted tree, on a bend of the Yarra. It stands in Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne.

trees.name: The Sugar Gum of Burnley Gardens

location.address: Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne Burnley campus, 500 Yarra Boulevard, Burnley VIC 3121

trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
Burnley Gardens' best known sugar gum is a table. The heritage-listed specimen on the entrance drive, dated to about 1887, dropped limbs once too often and came down in 2008; its timber was carved and the table unveiled in 2013. This is a different tree, and this one is alive.

It stands further into the grounds, and the City of Yarra recorded it on 4 October 2012, four years after that removal: 22 metres tall, 144 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which works out at roughly 4.52 metres of girth. That 144 is a width measured across the trunk, not a tape run around it. Particularly old, outstanding size, location of landscape context, in the register's own words. The age is the band and nothing more, over a hundred years, with no year behind it.

What says it is still standing is an iNaturalist record from September 2025, research grade, of a living Eucalyptus cladocalyx within about 25 metres of the register's point. Whether that photograph and that survey are the same trunk is inference rather than record, though nothing planted since 2008 could be this thick.

Sugar gums have a local reputation for shedding branches, which University of Melbourne researchers restated as recently as 2024. It is part of why an old one still upright in a public garden is worth the walk.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 229): dbh 144cm, height 22m, significance 'Particularly Old, Outstanding Size, Location of Landscape Context', surveyed 2012-10-04

iNaturalist observation 313237418, research grade, 2025-09-12, Eucalyptus cladocalyx (sugar gum) at -37.82679,145.01689, i.e. within about 25 metres of this register point: confirms species and continued life at essentially this exact spot as of September 2025.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 22 metres tall and about 4.52 metres round, standing further into the grounds than the garden's famous felled sugar gum. It stands in Burnley Gardens.

trees.name: The Yate of Burnley Gardens

location.address: Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne Burnley campus, 500 Yarra Boulevard, Burnley VIC 3121

trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
Yate grows wild on a strip of coast in the far south-west of Western Australia and almost nowhere else. This one is 18 metres tall and about four metres round, on the other side of the continent.

Eucalyptus cornuta takes its name from its buds, which taper to a long horn before the flowers open. A tree of this size well outside its range is the kind of thing a university's botanic garden accumulates: Burnley Gardens holds close to a thousand plant species across nine hectares, free to walk into, and the City of Yarra's register lists this one for its outstanding size and its place in the landscape.

Most of the trees on this page carry the register's blanket band of over a hundred years. This one got a narrower reading, 81 to 100 years at the survey on 4 October 2012, which puts the planting somewhere between roughly 1926 and 1945. Somebody looked and made a closer call, which is worth saying, because almost nowhere else on this page did they.

The measurements: 127 centimetres of diameter at breast height, so a girth of about 3.99 metres, converted from a diameter, which is what the register publishes rather than a circumference. Nothing outside that register names this tree. If you can date the Burnley yate, or have watched it flower here, tell us.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 230): dbh 127cm, height 18m, age band '81-100 years', significance 'Outstanding Size, Location of Landscape Context', surveyed 2012-10-04
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its buds tapering to a long horn before they flower, on a trunk about 4 metres round. It stands in Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne.

trees.name: The Bhutan Cypress of Burnley Gardens

location.address: Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne Burnley campus, 500 Yarra Boulevard, Burnley VIC 3121

trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
In the Himalaya this species passes 30 metres. Here it stands at 13. Cupressus torulosa, the Bhutan cypress, is a mountain conifer, and the one in Burnley Gardens has had an easier life than its relatives on a Himalayan slope: open ground, no competition for light, and a botanic garden looking after it. The City of Yarra's arborists recorded it on 4 October 2012 at 103 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to about 3.24 metres of girth, because the register publishes the width across a trunk rather than the distance around it. They tagged it rare or localised, and particularly old.

Burnley Gardens is nine hectares holding close to a thousand plant species, run by the University of Melbourne and free to walk into, and some of the oldest trees in the city are in it. This cypress is the sort of thing a register exists for: an unusual species, grown large, in a garden where somebody planted it deliberately and then nobody wrote down when.

That is the honest limit here. Nothing beyond the city's register names this individual tree, and its age is the register's blunt band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey, with no planting year attached. If you know when the Burnley cypress went in, tell us.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 163): dbh 103cm, height 13m, significance 'Rare or Localised, Particularly Old', surveyed 2012-10-04

Burnley Gardens (University of Melbourne Faculty of Science) confirmed as a nine-hectare public garden of nearly 1,000 plant species including some of the city's oldest trees; multiple independent descriptions (science.unimelb.edu.au, tripadvisor.com.au, gardendrum.com) corroborate the garden's identity and heritage-tree collection, but none names this individual Cupressus torulosa by species. Single-source on species/age for this specific tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its modest height, just 13 metres, short for a species that reaches 30 in the Himalaya, on open ground. It stands in Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne.

trees.name: The Osage Orange of Yarra Boulevard

location.address: Yarra Boulevard, near the Swan Street connection, Yarra Bend Park, Burnley VIC 3121

trees.access: Free, always open. Public parkland along Yarra Boulevard, part of Yarra Bend Park / the Boulevard Parklands, a well-used shared walking and cycling corridor along the Yarra River.
trees.transport: No tram or train stop immediately adjacent. Reachable via the Yarra River shared path or Yarra Boulevard itself; the nearest railway stations (Burnley, Victoria Park, or East Richmond) are roughly 2km away by path.
trees.story: Yarra Boulevard was built to give men work during the Depression. The tree beside it was already seventy years old. The Victorian Heritage Database's citation for the Boulevard Parklands records an Osage orange north-east of the point where the road meets Swan Street and dates it to the 1860s, which makes it around 160 now. Nothing else here has been dated that far back. The City of Yarra's register lists one at that spot too: 27 metres tall, 169 centimetres of diameter at breast height, about 5.31 metres of girth once converted, since the register gives the width across a trunk rather than the distance around it. Nobody has matched the two records trunk to trunk, but Osage orange is rare enough here that they almost certainly describe the same tree. The height is the odd part. Maclura pomifera is a thorny, low, awkward thing in its native Red River country of Texas and Oklahoma, and it rarely gets far past 20 metres anywhere. This one reached 27 on a river flat in Melbourne. Its wood is so dense and rot-resistant that Osage fence posts routinely outlast the wire stapled to them, which is part of why a tree from a small corner of America ended up on four continents. The road, by comparison, is barely ninety.
verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 227)

Victorian Heritage Database, 'The Boulevard Parklands' citation (vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/103863), cited via search: an Osage Orange 'situated ... to the north-east of the connection of Yarra Boulevard to Swan Street is listed on the Significant Tree Register', 'dating back to the 1860s'
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its unusual height, 27 metres, for a species that is normally low, thorny and awkward. It stands on Yarra Boulevard, near the Swan Street connection.

trees.name: The River Red Gum of Yarra Boulevard

location.address: Yarra Boulevard, Yarra Bend Park, Burnley VIC 3121

trees.access: Free, always open. Public parkland along Yarra Boulevard, part of Yarra Bend Park / the Boulevard Parklands.
trees.transport: No tram or train stop immediately adjacent. Reachable via the Yarra River shared path or Yarra Boulevard itself; the nearest railway stations (Burnley, Victoria Park, or East Richmond) are roughly 2km away by path.
trees.story: This one was probably never planted. The City of Yarra's register tags it remnant, its word for indigenous vegetation left standing rather than put in, and records 22 metres of height and 152 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to about 4.77 metres of girth, since the register publishes the width across a trunk rather than the way round it. Its age is the standard band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey. The Victorian Heritage Database's citation for these parklands says the remnant indigenous vegetation through the park is mostly river red gums, but it names no individual trees, so for this particular trunk the claim rests on the city's register alone. It stands about 1.4 kilometres along the Boulevard from the Osage orange and marks the far end of the second walk on this page, which begins in Burnley Gardens; the northern parks sit six or seven kilometres away. Eucalyptus camaldulensis is the tree of Australian watercourses, the species that held the banks of the Yarra before there was a Melbourne on them, and the Boulevard is a shared walking and cycling corridor along the river rather than a park you cut across. Come for the river as much as for the tree.

trees.name: The Southern Mahogany of Edinburgh Gardens

location.address: Edinburgh Gardens, off Alfred Crescent, Fitzroy North VIC 3068

trees.story:
This is a beach tree living in Fitzroy North. Eucalyptus botryoides belongs to the sandy, salt-touched country of the south-east Australian coast, behind dunes and around swamp margins, and it does not turn up this far inland on its own. Somebody carried it here and planted it, in a park laid out from 1862 whose heritage citation notes the number of mature specimen trees put in from that period onward. Which of those plantings this one belongs to is written down nowhere we can find.

The City of Yarra measured it in 2012 at 4.34 metres round and 25 metres tall, called it over a hundred years old then, and tagged it three ways on the significant trees register: particularly old, outstanding size, and its standing in the landscape. Over a hundred in 2012 makes it comfortably over 110 now.

It is also the third registered giant on this page within about 250 metres of Alfred Crescent, which is the useful thing to know if you are walking. The river red gum is roughly a hundred metres away and the holm oak a little beyond that, and the council's register lists seventeen more significant trees along the same stretch of grass.

One honest caveat: the register is the only document that names this individual tree. The heritage listing describes the park's tree collection and does not single it out.

trees.name: The Hoop Pine of Yarra Boulevard

location.address: Yarra Boulevard, Yarra Bend Park / Richmond Park, Burnley VIC 3121

trees.story:
The road this tree is named after was built by men on relief work. Yarra Boulevard was cut through Richmond Park in the 1930s by sustenance labourers, according to the heritage citation for the parkland, and the City of Yarra's register already had the hoop pine beside it down as over a hundred years old when it was updated in 2012. Whether this tree watched the road arrive is an open question. Nobody recorded when it was planted, and nothing ties it to the Boulevard's own avenue scheme, so the two dates sit there side by side without a document to join them.

What is certain: 3.46 metres round, 22 metres tall, in parkland that has been public since 1862, registered as particularly old and of outstanding size.

Araucaria cunninghamii is a rainforest tree from Queensland and northern New South Wales, an emergent that pushes its head above the canopy and holds its foliage in tufts at the ends of the branches, which gives an old one a candelabra look from a distance. It is planted all over southern Australia and is at home in none of it.

It stands about 260 metres from the osage orange already on this page and roughly 550 from the river red gum, so all three make one walk along the Boulevard. Only the register names this individual tree.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the rings of rough bark that band the trunk, 3.46 metres round, and foliage tufted at the branch ends 22 metres up. It stands on Yarra Boulevard, about 260 metres from the osage orange.

trees.name: The Peppercorn Tree of Madden Grove

location.address: Madden Grove, Richmond Park, Richmond VIC 3121

trees.story:
The ground this tree stands on was set aside in 1836, before Melbourne had a name worth arguing about. The Survey Paddock, as it was then, became Richmond Park and has been public land ever since, one of the earliest reservations in the city's history, and the peppercorn in Madden Grove is 3.55 metres round and 16 metres tall on that same ground.

Schinus molle is South American, from the dry Andean foothills, and it is the tree of colonial Australia more than almost any other import. It went in along stock routes, station tracks, rail sidings and school fences by the thousand, because it took drought, poor soil and neglect without complaint, and its weeping grey-green foliage is now so ordinary in the landscape that people assume it is native. It is not.

The City of Yarra's register put this one at over a hundred years old in 2012, which makes it over 110 now, and gave it the fullest set of tags of any tree checked here: particularly old, outstanding size, aesthetic value, and its place in the landscape. A second peppercorn of almost identical girth stands about 200 metres away.

Only the register names this individual tree; the heritage listing covers the park around it. Burnley station is about ten minutes' walk, and the river path brings you here from the Yarra Boulevard trees.

trees.name: The Lemon-scented Gum of Madden Grove

location.address: Madden Grove, Richmond Park, Richmond VIC 3121

trees.story:
Pick up one of the fallen leaves, crush it, and this tree gives itself away: the lemon-scented gum carries so much citronellal in its foliage that the oil is distilled commercially and sold as insect repellent. The smell is sharp, lemony and unmistakable, and it is the fastest identification of any tree on this page.

Corymbia citriodora comes from a modest patch of inland north Queensland, more than 1,500 kilometres from Richmond, and has been planted around the warm half of the world for its trunk: smooth, powdery, pale pink to white, shedding in sheets and clean of branches for most of its height. This one is 21 metres tall and 3.24 metres round, and the City of Yarra's register, which measured it in 2012, put it at 81 to 100 years then. That makes it somewhere around a century now, and the register carries it as particularly old and of outstanding size.

It stands in Madden Grove, on land held as public parkland since 1862 and reserved as the Survey Paddock a generation before that, about 250 metres from the peppercorn already mapped here. The two together make a second stop on the river walk that starts at the Yarra Boulevard trees, about two kilometres away along the river path.

Only the register names this specimen directly. Nobody has published a planting date for it.
